input.question: What makes treeline altitude (highest trees can grow) vary from place to place?
input.ground_truth: Water and heat availability. In general, a you get higher, both become more scarce until it's too cold and dry for any trees to grow. Of course, a mountain in the desert will hit the dryness limit sooner than one in the tropics, and one in Canada will hit the coldness limit sooner than one in Florida.

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you and I are looking at a big mountain with lots of trees at the bottom and then just rocks and snow higher up.

**Why can’t trees grow all the way to the top of the mountain?**

Well, as you go higher up a mountain, the air gets thinner. There’s less oxygen for the trees to breathe, and it gets really, really cold. Also, the soil is not as good for growing because it’s often just rocks or very thin dirt.

So, every mountain is a little bit different. Some mountains are warmer, some are colder, some have more good dirt, and some have less snow. That’s why the highest place where trees can grow (we call it the “treeline”) is in a different spot on every mountain. Sometimes it’s really high up, sometimes not so high, depending on how cold it is, how much sun the trees get, and how good the soil is for their roots.

Think of it like this: If you try to grow a plant in your sandbox at home, it might do well. But if you try to grow the same plant at the top of your house where it’s windy and cold, it won’t grow. Trees are the same way on mountains!
